Nests would fly out and become fully exposed to the weather elements once the leave are gone and make them vulnerable to sight from predators and other important living organisms. It’s now clear to me as to why very few animals call these trees their home. Also with the heavy amount of human traffic that walks by then each hour of each day would make it harder on animals to feel comfortable raising their young in such a dense populated spot. description:
The red maple leaf (Acer rubrum) belongs to the kingdom Plantae and is a seeded vascular angiosperm in the family Sapindaceae. An angiosperm is a plant that produces flowers and seeds that are enclosed in a carpel, which is presented in the image. A carpel is the reproductive organ of the flower, containing a style, stigma, and an ovary. This maple leaf is a native deciduous tree that is most common in wetter habitats such as swamps, poor dry soils, wetlands, and forest environments. They are distributed across eastern North America, but most commonly found along the Atlantic coast of North America. Many species are found in the east such as Texas and Florida due to the warm temperatures.  In the appropriate habitat, they are fast-growing and weak wooded. They grow in a variety of fall colors, consisting of brown, red, green, and orange. Additionally, they typically live as old as 75-100 years old. Yet, they are commonly eaten by deer, dragonflies, and are a food source for the larvae that belongs to several species of butterflies.

description:
"The U.S. Forest service recognizes it as the most abundant native tree in eastern North America.[4] 

It is used commercially on a small scale for maple syrup production as well as for its medium to high quality lumber.

Red maple lumber contains a greater percentage of "curly" (aka "flame"/"fiddleback") figure, which is prized by musical instrument/custom furniture makers, as well as the veneer industry. As a soft maple, the wood tends to shrink more during the drying process than with the hard maples.

Red maple is also used for the production of maple syrup, though the hard maples Acer saccharum (sugar maple) and Acer nigrum (black maple) are more commonly utilized. One study compared the sap and syrup from the sugar maple with those of the red maple, as well as those of the Acer saccharinum (silver maple), Acer negundo (boxelder), and Acer platanoides (Norway maple), and all were found to be equal in sweetness, flavor, and quality. However, the buds of red maple and other soft maples emerge much earlier in the spring than the sugar maple, and after sprouting chemical makeup of the sap changes, imparting an undesirable flavor to the syrup. This being the case, red maple can only be tapped for syrup before the buds emerge, making the season very short.[9]

Native Americans used red maple bark as a wash for inflamed eyes and cataracts, and as a remedy for hives and muscular aches. They also would brew tea from the inner bark to treat coughs and diarrhea. Pioneers made cinnamon-brown and black dyes from a bark extract, and iron sulphate could be added to the tannin from red maple bark in order to make ink.

Red maple is a medium quality firewood, possessing less heat energy,  than other hardwoods such as Ash,  Oak, or Birch. 

Red maple is far more abundant today than when Europeans first arrived in North America. It only contributed minimally to old growth upland forests, and would only form same-species stands in riparian zones.[9] The density of the tree in many of these areas has increased 6- to 7-fold, and this trend seems to be continuing, all of which is due to human factors, mainly continued heavy logging and a recent trend of young, shrubby forests recovering from past human disturbances. Also, the decline of American elm and American chestnut due to introduced diseases has contributed to its spread. Red maple dominates such sites, but largely disappears until it only has a sparse presence by the time a forest is mature. This species is in fact a vital part of forest regeneration in the same way that paper birch is.

The red maple is used as a food source by several forms of wildlife. Elk and white-tailed deer in particular use the current season's growth of red maple as an important source of winter food. Several Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths) utilize the leaves as food, including larvae of the rosy maple moth (Dryocampa rubicunda)."

Native
1014

"The U.S. Forest service recognizes it as the most abundant native tree in eastern North America.[4] 

It is used commercially on a small scale for maple syrup production as well as for its medium to high quality lumber.

Red maple lumber contains a greater percentage of "curly" (aka "flame"/"fiddleback") figure, which is prized by musical instrument/custom furniture makers, as well as the veneer industry. As a soft maple, the wood tends to shrink more during the drying process than with the hard maples.

Red maple is also used for the production of maple syrup, though the hard maples Acer saccharum (sugar maple) and Acer nigrum (black maple) are more commonly utilized. One study compared the sap and syrup from the sugar maple with those of the red maple, as well as those of the Acer saccharinum (silver maple), Acer negundo (boxelder), and Acer platanoides (Norway maple), and all were found to be equal in sweetness, flavor, and quality. However, the buds of red maple and other soft maples emerge much earlier in the spring than the sugar maple, and after sprouting chemical makeup of the sap changes, imparting an undesirable flavor to the syrup. This being the case, red maple can only be tapped for syrup before the buds emerge, making the season very short.[9]

Native Americans used red maple bark as a wash for inflamed eyes and cataracts, and as a remedy for hives and muscular aches. They also would brew tea from the inner bark to treat coughs and diarrhea. Pioneers made cinnamon-brown and black dyes from a bark extract, and iron sulphate could be added to the tannin from red maple bark in order to make ink.

Red maple is a medium quality firewood, possessing less heat energy, than other hardwoods such as Ash, Oak, or Birch. 

Red maple is far more abundant today than when Europeans first arrived in North America. It only contributed minimally to old growth upland forests, and would only form same-species stands in riparian zones.[9] The density of the tree in many of these areas has increased 6- to 7-fold, and this trend seems to be continuing, all of which is due to human factors, mainly continued heavy logging and a recent trend of young, shrubby forests recovering from past human disturbances. Also, the decline of American elm and American chestnut due to introduced diseases has contributed to its spread. Red maple dominates such sites, but largely disappears until it only has a sparse presence by the time a forest is mature. This species is in fact a vital part of forest regeneration in the same way that paper birch is.

The red maple is used as a food source by several forms of wildlife. Elk and white-tailed deer in particular use the current season's growth of red maple as an important source of winter food. Several Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths) utilize the leaves as food, including larvae of the rosy maple moth (Dryocampa rubicunda)."

Red maple trees are perennial plants.

These trees begin flowering  at the end of winter and into early spring, typically from about March to May.

Red maple trees have leaves with 3 or 5 lobes and sinuses that are irregularly toothed. They can be distinguished from other similar looking maple trees because they have red stems on their leaves. 

Red Maple trees occur in hardiness zones 3-9 which is all zones of the United States, thus it occurs in many habitats. It is a generalist species that takes advantage of a wide variety of resources across different habitats.

The berries of red maple trees are often eaten by bunnies like the cottontail rabbit but this is not harmful to the tree.

Red Maple
•	Annual or perennial: Perennial
•	Season: flowers in early spring, from February to April depending on location
•	Description: One of the most prevalent trees in the eastern US. Easily recognized by its leaf shape, with jagged edges and three primary “prongs”. Sugar and Black Maples, while they have similar leaf shapes, have smoother edges, and Silver Maple leaves have a much different, more star-like shape. Also known for their fall colors, with leaves turning bright red earlier than many other trees.
•	Habitat: A wide variety. Also called “swamp maple”, and at home in such wet areas, but also succeeds in poor and dry soils. Also does well in disturbed habitats and is not very common in climax forests. 
•	Predator/Parasitism: The Rosy Maple Moth prefers maple trees as a host for its eggs.

description: Today I saw a red maple tree (Acer rubrum). The weather today was mostly cloudy with a high of 57° F and a low of 47° F. I could tell this was a red maple because of the distinct palmate 5 lobed leaf. That firstly told me this was a maple tree. This tree was kind of hard to take pictures of because all of the leaves were high up where I couldn't reach. So I included some zoomed in photos of the leaves, that's why they aren't a good quality photo. The part that told me it was a red maple tree was the fact that it had smooth bark. Something I found extremely interesting was the fact that this tree had a lot of damage at the base of the trunk. I believe this was caused by male white tail deer (Odocoileus virginianus) rubbing their antlers on the tree. It was really cool to get to see this evidence of the deer, even though it sucks for the tree.
